item.title: Cardi B Lands Billboard Canada’s First Global Woman Of The Year Award
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Cardi B will return to Toronto for a new global honor after an arena run that put her among the world's top touring acts.
item.content:encoded:
Cardi B will receive Billboard Canada’s first Global Woman of the Year award at its Women In Music event in Toronto on November 24.

The organizer announced her selection Friday, October 16. She will accept the honor at Rebel, six years after she won Billboard’s U.S. Woman of the Year title. The announcement credits her with 46 songs on the Canadian Hot 100, including eight top 10 hits.

The nod also follows a strong year on the road. Pollstar’s midyear report ranked Cardi seventh among the world’s top touring acts, with a $72.1 million gross from her Little Miss Drama Tour.

That run took her through North American arenas from February through April. By the tour’s halfway point, she had sold 209,622 tickets across its first 17 shows and grossed more than $32 million.

She toured behind her second album, Am I the Drama?, which came out in September 2025. The new award brings her back to Canada after that arena run included stops in Vancouver, Toronto and Hamilton.

She also sold out two shows at the Forum in Inglewood, a first for a female rapper, her tour promoter said.

Her first Woman of the Year honor came in 2020, when “WAP” with Megan Thee Stallion spent four weeks atop the Hot 100. That December, the ceremony took place virtually during the coronavirus pandemic.

At the 2020 show, she tied the honor to how her work had grown. “I want to be the best I can at anything that I do,” she said. “There’s hope for your dreams.”

That earlier honor recognized her music, live shows, cultural reach and activism throughout the year.

Her first Grammy came in 2019, the year before her first Billboard honor. She became the first solo woman to win Best Rap Album, taking the prize for her debut, Invasion of Privacy. Her career tally now stands at one win and 11 nominations. “Outside” earned her a Best Rap Performance nod in 2026.

The Toronto event will also honor Live Nation Canada’s Melissa Bubb-Clarke as Executive of the Year. Kristy Fletcher of MusiCounts, CARAS and the Juno Awards will receive its Impact Award.

Tickets for the November 24 event are on sale.

item.title: Young Thug’s YSL Trial Headed To Netflix?
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: Young Thug's judicial ordeal gains a Hollywood dimension as a forthcoming Netflix production promises unprecedented scrutiny of the YSL prosecution.
item.content:encoded:
Young Thug‘s sprawling Georgia racketeering case could become the subject of a new Netflix documentary titled “Young Thug on Trial,” reportedly scheduled for 2027.

The proposed production would revisit one of the most closely watched criminal proceedings in Hip-Hop history, a case that brought questions about rap lyrics, artistic expression and the criminal justice system into the national spotlight.

However, the reported Netflix announcement and 2027 release date still require independent confirmation. No filmmakers, interview participants or production details have been established from the information provided.

The project has now received a significant confirmation from someone directly involved in the case.

Fulton County Superior Court Judge Paige Whitaker, who presided over the trial, discussed the documentary during an interview published Oct. 13 on Class E’s “What You Need to Know” program.

“Netflix and Passion Pictures are doing a documentary of the YSL trial,” Whitaker said. “I was interviewed for that documentary and it is supposed to air sometime next year.” 

The judge also indicated that an exclusivity agreement limits what she can discuss before the documentary premieres.

According to published reports, the approximately 90-minute production will be directed by Shianne Brown, with Kari Lia and Hamish Fergusson serving as executive producers. The film is expected to explore Young Thug’s rise from Atlanta’s music scene and the prosecution’s allegations that YSL operated as a criminal street gang.

The underlying case began in 2022 when Young Thug, whose legal name is Jeffery Williams, was indicted alongside other defendants under Georgia’s racketeering statute.

The proceedings became notorious for their extraordinary length, courtroom disruptions and disputes over the introduction of rap lyrics as evidence. Prosecutors argued that certain lyrics helped establish connections to alleged criminal activity. Defense attorneys challenged the implications of treating artistic expression as evidence of wrongdoing.

Young Thug ultimately entered guilty and no contest pleas in October 2024. His sentence allowed him to leave custody subject to 15 years of probation and other conditions.

The forthcoming film will not be the first documentary to examine the case. ABC News Studios released “Rap Trap: Hip-Hop on Trial” in 2023, examining the prosecution and the broader debate over criminalizing rap lyrics. 

Still, Whitaker’s participation gives the new production a potentially valuable perspective from inside the courtroom.

No precise premiere date has been disclosed, and Netflix has not independently confirmed the complete release details in the official materials I located.

For Young Thug, the courtroom proceedings may be over, but their consequences continue to shape his public story. The next chapter will unfold before a streaming audience, revisiting a legal battle that forced Hip-Hop to confront how its words can be interpreted far beyond the recording studio.

item.title: IShowSpeed Joins Obama-Backed “The Eyes Of Ghana” As Producer
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: IShowSpeed joined an Obama-backed Ghana documentary as a producer, helping promote a film about saving endangered archives.
item.content:encoded:
IShowSpeed joined “The Eyes Of Ghana” as a producer, helping promote the Obama-backed film’s one-night theater release to his audience.

Breakwater Studios and Higher Ground announced the new partnership earlier this week. The streamer shared the trailer for the October 28, 2026, event across the United States and Canada. He received a producer credit under Darren Watkins, while Barack and Michelle Obama served as executive producers.

The new film credit extended his media work beyond livestreaming. He had also bought a Miami-area warehouse to build a content studio.

Director Ben Proudfoot’s film centers on Chris Hesse, the Ghanaian cameraman who filmed his country’s independence and kept its images safe for decades. Hesse worked for Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana’s first president. After Nkrumah’s overthrow in 1966, he protected more than 1,300 reels that recorded African independence and visits by world leaders.

“I’m humbled by his legacy and proud to help bring his story to my community,” Speed said of Hesse in the announcement.

The film had screened at festivals in 2025. Speed’s new role put his reach behind this year’s theater push.

The work went well beyond the footage that reached the screen. Earlier this year, Proudfoot told Ghana’s national broadcaster, GBC, that the film used about 15 minutes from the archive. He estimated that more than 300 hours of original negatives remained in a London vault.

Proudfoot warned that age and chemical decay threatened the footage. He called on government bodies, cultural groups and international partners to help save it.

Filmmaker Anita Afonu explained why she wanted the images back in Ghana.

“Our work is to bring them home to the people they belong to, and home is Ghana,” she told The Produced.

The negatives had gone to London because Ghana lacked the facilities to store them, Afonu said. She wanted people in Ghana to have digital copies. As a film student, she had studied European, Soviet and Hollywood work while films by earlier Ghanaian directors stayed out of reach.

The documentary also follows the restoration of Accra’s Rex Theater as a place to show Hesse’s work. Afonu told the Hawai‘i International Film Festival that she hoped the film’s success would draw support for the full archive.

item.title: Chad Hugo Fires Back At Pharrell Over Nearly 50 Neptunes Sessions
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Chad Hugo challenged Pharrell's dismissal bid with claims about studio work, missing records and disputed song credits.
item.content:encoded:
Chad Hugo fired back at Pharrell Williams’ bid to toss his copyright case, citing nearly 50 studio sessions from 2019 through 2021.

According to Rolling Stone, Hugo said Pharrell and music firms held records he needed to name released songs. He said he sought books and royalty statements from 2021 through 2024 but got almost nothing.

“Defendants ask the court to write Chad Hugo out of The Neptunes on the pleadings, before a single document has been produced,” the filing said, Rolling Stone reported.

Hugo cited EarthGang’s “U Gotta.” He claimed his name was dropped from its credits even though the artists said he helped make it.

Pharrell moved on October 6 to throw out claims he argued left the songs and rights unclear. His lawyer, Edwin F. McPherson, said Hugo should name the works he claimed to have helped make.

“They are asking that he simply identify what ‘works’ he claims to have co-authored. This is exclusively within his own knowledge,” McPherson argued in the earlier filing.

In an earlier version of the suit, Hugo named eight works and left room for other music. Pharrell’s lawyers argued that the open-ended claims left them unable to tell which songs or recordings he meant.

Pharrell’s role was central to how the track was pitched to the public. EarthGang’s PR firm, twnty three, called “U Gotta” a Pharrell-produced record in its October 30, 2024 release for “Perfect Fantasy.” It also named him as the featured guest.

The U.S. Copyright Office explains that a song’s music and lyrics are protected separately from its recording, and those rights can have different owners and licensing deals. Pharrell’s demand for clarity therefore reached two questions: which works Hugo claimed, and which rights he said he owned in each.

Hugo also sought the books for The Neptunes and N.E.R.D. to learn what he was owed. He claimed he had not been fully paid for the band’s 2017 album “No One Ever Really Dies.” Hugo alleged that his missing pay for that album could reach $1 million.

Pharrell’s lawyers did not immediately respond to Rolling Stone’s request for comment.

item.title: YK Osiris Stopped By Deshae Frost After Slap Feud
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: YK Osiris’ rivalry with Deshae Frost reached a new result after an in-ring slap helped set up their Brand Risk 16 bout.
item.content:encoded:
YK Osiris lost to Deshae Frost by a second-round technical knockout at Brand Risk 16, according to the promotion’s official result post.

The finish came on Adin Ross’ October 16 card at the Brand Risk Warehouse in Miami, where the two met in the co-main event. MMA Fighting listed the stoppage at 2:59 of the second round.

The bout grew out of a confrontation at an earlier Brand Risk show. In a September 24 post, the promoter said YK Osiris slapped Deshae Frost inside the ring at Brand Risk 15. The promotion said the slap led to the October 16 booking.

Brand Risk kept the dispute in its fight-week buildup with a clip it described as YK Osiris explaining the slap. The caption said he had warned Deshae Frost that he would hit him the next time they met.

The pair had also boxed each other well before that confrontation. Their earlier match appeared on PlaqueBoyMaxLive’s YouTube channel in July 2025, more than a year before the slap became the basis for their latest booking.

YK Osiris brought more Brand Risk experience into the latest matchup. He lost to Scam Likely by TKO in the second round in Miami on January 23. That followed an April 2025 meeting with the same opponent that ended in a unanimous-decision loss, according to YTBoxRec’s bout history.

His August 22 meeting with Bob Menery ended as a no contest after one round at the Austin McBroom versus FaZe Temper event in Miami. That left YK Osiris returning to the ring against a familiar opponent when he and Deshae Frost met again Friday.

Ross’ Miami event mixed entertainers and athletes on the same card, with boxing among the featured competitions. Former NBA players Michael Beasley and Delonte West also fought, with Beasley winning by first-round TKO. The promotion placed YK Osiris and Deshae Frost above that matchup in the co-main slot.

His public interest in boxing stretches back years. AllHipHop reported on his glove-on clash with Lil Tjay in May 2020. Afterward, YK Osiris offered $30,000 to $40,000 for another round and called out Polo G for a possible fight.

item.title: Diddy Was Allegedly In Extreme Danger: Did A Jamaican Gangster Force His Prison Transfer?
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: A chilling warning from an AllHipHop source raises new questions about Diddy's safety following his transfer from Fort Dix.
item.content:encoded:
Sean “Diddy” Combs reportedly moved from Fort Dix to Allenwood, but an insider’s chilling warning raises questions about what really happened behind bars.

Let me tell you guys something! This Diddy situation just took another turn, and I have been sitting on some information that might explain why.

Ever since reports surfaced about an alleged confrontation between Sean “Diddy” Combs and a notorious Jamaican drug lord, I have been hearing some disturbing things. And when I say disturbing, I mean the kind of stuff that makes you wonder whether Diddy was in much more danger than the public realized.

Now, before we go any further, let me explain something about the man allegedly involved.

His name is Christopher “Dudus” Coke, and if you know anything about Jamaican organized crime, you already know that name carries serious weight. Coke was once the leader of the infamous Shower Posse, a criminal organization with roots in Jamaica and connections to international drug trafficking.

The Shower Posse earned its notorious reputation through extreme violence, including shootings involving automatic weapons. This was not some little neighborhood crew. These were serious people operating in a very dangerous world.

And according to the rumors circulating around Diddy’s prison experience, he may have found himself on the wrong side of someone with that kind of history.

Now, let’s talk about Fort Dix.

As previously reported, Diddy was incarcerated at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey, a federal low-security correctional institution. There have been allegations about his lifestyle behind bars, including access to alcohol, massages, unauthorized cell phones and other privileges that ordinary inmates are not supposed to enjoy.

Some of these claims remain disputed or unverified, so I am not going to present every prison rumor as established fact.

However, the reports certainly created the impression that Diddy was attempting to maintain some version of his celebrity lifestyle while serving federal time.

And that can create problems.

Think about it. You have an internationally famous Hip-Hop mogul entering a prison environment where other inmates have their own relationships, hierarchies and unwritten rules. Suddenly, there is tremendous attention on this one individual.

Could that attention have disrupted arrangements other inmates had enjoyed for years?

That’s one possibility. But I have not seen evidence establishing that as the cause of any confrontation.

My Source Had A Chilling Warning About Diddy

Now, here is the part that really caught my attention.

I received information from a source who was adamant that Diddy could have been in serious danger if the reported confrontation involved Dudus Coke.

This is what the source told me:

“Hey… I saw your post on Diddy. The dude Diddy got into a fight with in jail is the TRUTH… Dudus is a Jamaican Gangster LEGEND. Real talk, Diddy life expectancy just dropped. Keep up with that story.”

That’s a pretty chilling assessment.

Notice that my source was not simply talking about a fight. The concern was about who Diddy allegedly had a confrontation with and what that could mean moving forward.

There have been conflicting accounts of what actually happened. Some reports described a physical altercation, while others downplayed the situation as a minor disagreement.

Former Diddy associate Roger Bonds also weighed in, claiming to have information from people inside the prison. His account suggested that the confrontation was not nearly as dramatic as some reports indicated.

So, what really happened?

We still do not know for certain.

But now we have another development to consider.

Did Diddy’s Prison Transfer Have Something To Do With His Safety?

Diddy has reportedly been transferred from Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low in Pennsylvania.

And I have questions!

Was this a routine administrative decision? Was it related to disciplinary issues? Or did prison officials determine that the situation at Fort Dix had become too dangerous?

I cannot confirm that his alleged encounter with Coke caused the transfer. Federal prison transfers can happen for several reasons, including security concerns, institutional needs and inmate classification.

But the timing certainly raises questions worth asking.

There were reports about Diddy spending time in special housing, commonly referred to as solitary confinement. There were also reports about an outside medical evaluation following a head injury.

Neither development, by itself, proves that someone was targeting him.

Still, taken together, these reports have fueled speculation about what was really happening behind those walls.

My source offered another warning:

“If he stayed there…Diddy might as well never come back to NY”

Now, that statement is serious.

The implication is that a dispute involving someone with a powerful criminal reputation could potentially follow Diddy beyond the prison walls.

However, I want to be very clear. I have no independent evidence that Coke or anyone associated with him has threatened Diddy outside prison, or that any plan exists to harm him.

That distinction matters.

Diddy May Have A Better Situation At Allenwood

Assuming the reported transfer is accurate, Diddy will now have to adjust to a different federal prison environment.

And perhaps that is exactly what he needs.

FCI Allenwood Low is a low-security federal correctional institution. It is not a luxury facility, and there is no reason to assume Diddy will automatically receive better treatment there.

However, a change of environment could provide some distance from whatever tensions may have developed at Fort Dix.

There is also the issue of his projected release date, which reportedly shifted further into 2028. That does not necessarily mean additional time was added to his original sentence. Federal projected release dates can change because of administrative calculations, good-conduct credits and other factors.

But here’s what I keep coming back to.

Diddy was once one of the most powerful men in Hip-Hop. He helped shape an entire era of music, fashion, television and entertainment. Now, he is navigating a federal prison system where his fame and fortune cannot guarantee his safety.

And if the allegations about his confrontation with Dudus Coke have any truth to them, the situation could have been more serious than people initially believed.

I do not wish harm on Diddy or anybody else. That is one reason I hesitated to publish some of what I was hearing.

But when my source started talking about life expectancy and the possibility of problems following Diddy back to New York, I took notice.

For now, perhaps the move to Allenwood gives Diddy an opportunity to start fresh.

New prison. New surroundings. New relationships.

I guess he has to make some new friends now, right?

One thing is certain: the public still does not have a complete, independently verified account of what happened at Fort Dix.

And until we do, the questions are not going away.

The Legacy Of Dudus Coke And The Shower Posse

The history behind Christopher “Dudus” Coke helps explain why his name inspires such strong reactions. Coke rose to prominence in Kingston’s Tivoli Gardens community, inheriting influence associated with his father, Lester Lloyd Coke, also known as Jim Brown. The Shower Posse became notorious during the violent Jamaican political and criminal conflicts of the 1980s, with operations extending into the United States. Christopher Coke was extradited to America in 2010 and later received a 23-year federal prison sentence in 2012. His criminal history is documented, but that history does not establish the truth of allegations involving Diddy.

What do you think? Was Diddy’s reported transfer simply routine prison business, or could there be a much bigger story behind it? Comment your thoughts below.

item.title: Bun B Thanks Drake For Sending Money & Fans Back His Way
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Bun B credited Drake's "Solar Eclipse" sample with fresh income and renewed streams for "Get Throwed," extending their long rap bond.
item.content:encoded:
Bun B credited Drake with bringing fresh money and listeners to “Get Throwed” after the Houston classic landed inside “Solar Eclipse.”

The UGK veteran described two payoffs in a new Rolling Stone interview: income from the sample and a rise in streams for his own recording as fans went looking for the source.

“Not only is there revenue from having your song attached to a Drake song, but also, people rediscover the original record,” Bun B said.

Drake and Don Toliver reworked Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” for their collaboration, drawing on the bass line from “Get Throwed.”

Drake had already sampled Bun B’s song on “N 2 Deep” in 2021, so the new placement extended a connection between their catalogs.

Their relationship began long before that sample. Bun B joined Drake and Lil Wayne on “Uptown” from the 2009 mixtape So Far Gone, giving the young Toronto artist a major Southern co-sign.

The pair also shared stages in Houston. Drake later appeared on Bun B’s Trill OG.

In a 2010 interview, Bun B explained that he recognized the younger rapper’s drive and saw a parallel with UGK’s blend of hard-edged stories and melodic hooks.

“Get Throwed” came from Bun B’s first solo album, Trill, released in 2005. Mr. Lee produced the track, which brought together Pimp C, Jay-Z, Jeezy and Z-Ro alongside Bun B.

That solo chapter grew out of Pimp C’s imprisonment. Bun B later told Jesse Thorn on “Bullseye” that he had suddenly taken on jobs his partner usually handled, from choosing beats to sequencing the album. Keeping UGK moving meant learning how to carry the whole recording process himself.

Two decades later, that work reached another audience through a song that entered the Hot 100 at No. 5. “Solar Eclipse” arrived on streaming services October 2 after its earlier appearance in Drake’s “FOMO” film.

Bun B also backed Drake’s ability to withstand the backlash surrounding his feud with Kendrick Lamar. He praised the rapper’s persistence and argued that his audience had remained strong despite people counting him out.

Bun B said he planned to release new music in 2027.

item.title: Michael Che Explains Why “Shot In Minnesota” Avoids Naming Shooting Victims
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Michael Che explained the choices behind "Shot in Minnesota" as a local comedian questioned one joke and praised his support.
item.content:encoded:
Michael Che said he avoided naming victims of Minnesota killings in his new Netflix special to address frustration around violence while keeping the focus on comedy.

That backdrop included George Floyd’s 2020 death and the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents earlier this year.

The “Saturday Night Live” star explained the choice to MPR News after “Michael Che: Shot in Minnesota” arrived on October 13. He taped the hour at First Avenue in Minneapolis over four shows in August, but its title carried a broader message.

“It’s not necessarily about those people individually,” Che said. “You have to be very careful, and making jokes about things like that, and keeping the mood up for a special, you know, it is a comedy special. I didn’t want to invoke those names in a joking way and sort of kill what we were trying to do. But it’s really more about the frustration of what’s happening, as opposed to the nuts and bolts of everything that’s ever happened.”

Che also discussed the pressure on Black comedians in a new Vanity Fair interview. He recalled arriving at “SNL” in 2013 as its only Black writer and finding his footing with help from Kenan Thompson and Jay Pharoah.

“Coming here, it was tough because I was the only Black writer here,” he said. He became the first Black co-anchor of “Weekend Update” in 2014.

The subject has remained part of his public commentary. In May, AllHipHop covered his criticism of the white writers behind Shane Gillis’ material at Kevin Hart’s Netflix roast.

Che told The Ringer that he initially wanted to join the roast out of respect for Hart and Gillis. He said travel around his “SNL” schedule and the prospect of harsh jokes about friends made it less appealing.

He also pushed back on the idea that Black comedians needed to speak for everyone. He argued that they could serve their own audiences without winning over every viewer, and explained why he still valued his network platform.

Che said “SNL” gave him a live audience on 20 Saturdays each year, with the chance to create moments people remembered. The show also left room for him to make specials, write and produce his own work.

“I’m from poverty, man. We don’t just give up jobs,” he said.

item.title: Outkast’s Ovrkast Lawsuit Draws Pushback From Original Interviewer
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Outkast's case against Ovrkast prompted debate over a quoted interview and the personal and business costs of changing a rap name.
item.content:encoded:
Outkast‘s trademark fight with Ovrkast drew criticism from Andre Gee, the journalist whose interview with the younger rapper became part of the case against his stage name.

Gee told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution that the 2025 conversation focused on Ovrkast’s rise as an independent artist. He never expected a casual discussion to become material in a lawsuit.

“To see the systems of the industry kind of infiltrate that is just disappointing,” Gee said, describing Hip-Hop’s roots as a counterculture.

The dispute began long before those new comments. As AllHipHop reported, High Schoolers LLC, the trademark company controlled by Big Boi and André 3000, sued Ovrkast in Georgia federal court on September 16.

The complaint cited his July 2025 Rolling Stone interview, in which he described people misreading Ovrkast as Outkast. The company presented that account as support for its claim that listeners confused the two names.

Ovrkast had publicly explained a different inspiration years earlier. In a 2022 KQED profile, the Oakland rapper-producer traced his name to rainy days spent indoors drawing and finding music. He described the weather, creativity and calm as connected parts of his identity.

The AJC also heard a defense of Outkast’s position from trademark attorney Dayna Thomas. She said owners needed to enforce their rights, while cautioning that similar sound or meaning alone did not settle whether one name infringed on another.

Fellow attorney Lee Morin viewed Ovrkast’s earlier description of confused readers as an admission that could strengthen the group’s argument.

Journalist Yoh Phillips emphasized the burden on the smaller artist. Rebranding meant changes to websites, social accounts and merchandise, with costs that extended well beyond picking another word.

High Schoolers alleged that Ovrkast agreed to switch to Overkxst by July 15, then failed to complete the change.

The company acknowledged that he never signed the proposed settlement, but argued that their lawyers negotiated a binding deal.

It sought damages, a ban on the disputed name, and the destruction of branded materials.

Ovrkast disputed copying the duo in a statement to Rolling Stone in September. He said he built his name independently, expressed respect for Outkast and hoped for a resolution that would let him continue his own career.

His earlier account tied that name to a feeling he wanted to preserve. “I always loved rain and Oakland hoodie weather,” he told KQED. “That’s where the idea of Ovrkast. came from.”

item.title: 50 Cent Trolls Diddy’s Allenwood Move With Outrageous Baby-Oil Toy Video
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: 50 Cent paired news of Diddy's Allenwood prison move with a crude toy video, adding a fresh jab to their long-running feud.
item.content:encoded:
50 Cent mocked Diddy’s move to Allenwood with an Instagram post that paired the prison news with a crude baby-oil toy video.

The rapper posted the two-slide jab Friday, October 16. The first slide showed a screenshot of TMZ’s report on Diddy’s move.

The next showed a video toy with Diddy’s likeness bent forward beside a pink bottle labeled baby oil.

The baby oil goes in the contraptions butt, and outcome bubbles.

The clip, from a TikTok account known as thediddybubble, cuts to a woman laughing with a hand over her mouth because the toy of Diddy is so crazy.

50 Cent wrote, “Diddy on the move, he gonna turn up in this next joint on gang !” He added tags for his Branson Cognac and Le Chemin du Roi brands.

The post went up after news broke that Diddy had left FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey for FCI Allenwood Low in Pennsylvania. Federal prison officials confirmed the move to ABC News. They declined to give a reason, citing privacy, safety and security.

The two men’s feud dates back 20 years. In 2006, 50 Cent wanted Mase to join G-Unit. Diddy wouldn’t let Mase out of his Bad Boy deal. They traded jabs before Chris Lighty confirmed a cease-fire that September.

50 Cent later took his interest in Diddy’s troubles beyond social media. He helped make “Sean Combs: The Reckoning” for Netflix as an executive producer. Alexandria Stapleton directed the four-part series. Netflix began streaming all four parts on December 2, 2025.

The film drew on interviews with former Bad Boy figures, people who sued Diddy and jurors from his trial. It also used footage shot in the days before his September 2024 arrest. Stapleton said the team obtained that footage legally and had the rights to use it. Its final episode, “Blink Again,” won an Emmy for its editing this year.

This week, 50 Cent discussed the film on “Jimmy Kimmel Live.” He joked that an unpaid cameraman had handed over Diddy’s footage. Longtime videographer Michael Oberlies had disputed that account and denied that a fee dispute drove the footage’s release.

Diddy, whose legal name is Sean Combs, is serving a 50-month federal prison term. A jury found him guilty of moving people across state lines for paid sex. It cleared him of sex trafficking and racketeering conspiracy.

His team acknowledged the move Friday. A representative told ABC News, “Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption.”
